messages.content: Dear Dr. Garry, It has been several months since we last spoke — I hope you are well. NBC News correspondent Janis MacKey Frayer was granted a tour of the WIV BSL 4 labs on Friday — the first international correspondent to do so since the Covid outbreak. She will file for The Today Show tomorrow, Monday. I know from your NATURE article on the origins of the virus and our conversations that you and your co-authors concluded that it is improbable that the virus was manufactured in a lab. Because that was several months ago now (feels like a lifetime ago!), I wanted to get an update from you as to whether you still feel that it is impossible or improbable that the outbreak started from the WIV labs in any form. (Manufactured or just “escaped” due to an error of some sort.) I know you may very well feel that this has been “asked and answered” many times, but in the interests of accuracy I wanted to check in before this airs tomorrow morning. Kind regards, Amy. Amy Perrette, Producer, NBC News London

I got this last night: Dear Dr. Rambaut, I hope this message finds you well. I am writing from the PLOS Publication Ethics team to ask if you might be able to help advise us on a pending post-publication case involving the above PLOS Pathogens article. Several concerns have been raised about the article, including about apparent overlap or redundancy with other publications and about the availability of the underlying data. The authors have worked with us to address these issues, and based on the outcome of these discussions we have prepared the attached notice draft. However, before we proceed further or decide whether this would be suitable for a Correction (vs. a different type of editorial notice), we are seeking to have the underlying data reviewed. The underlying data were not provided or evaluated during the pre-publication peer review, and the outcome of this post-publication case will depend on whether the data support the reported results and conclusions, and whether they fully address PLOS' Data Availability requirements. The data in question include pangolin SARS-CoV-2 sequencing data available through NCBI as well as gap-filling amplicon and contig sequencing data as provided in the attached files. In essence, we are seeking expert input as to whether the dataset provided is complete (per community data reporting standards for this type of study, and per the results reported in the article), whether the data are overall satisfactory, and whether the data provide clear and adequate support for the article's results and conclusions. If there are any concerns about the dataset or how the data align with the reported claims, we would also appreciate input on whether the issue could be addressed via a Correction or whether it has substantial implications for the reliability and/or validity of the article's conclusions. One of the PLOS Pathogens Editors-in-Chief suggested you may be able to recommend possible reviewers (e.g. bioinformaticians or viral genomics researchers) who could help with this data review. Do you have any suggestions? Alternatively, if you would be able to help review the data yourself, we would also be truly grateful for that level of support. Thank you in advance for any help you can offer at this time. If you have any questions about this case or this request, please email me and I would be happy to provide any clarifications. Thank you for your time and consideration. I look forward to hearing from you. Best regards, Renee. Renee Hoch, Ph.D., Senior Editor, Team Manager Publication Ethics, PLOS

[OCR unclear, continuing from a prior message:] https://www.wsj.com/articles/the-science-suggests-a-wuhan-lab-leak-11622995184 Specifically: In the case of the gain-of-function supercharge, other sequences could have been spliced into this same site. Instead of a CGG-CGG (known as “double CGG”) that tells the protein factory to make two arginine amino acids in a row, you'll obtain equal lethality by splicing any one of 35 of the other two-word combinations for double arginine. If the insertion takes place naturally, say through recombination, then one of those 35 other sequences is far more likely to appear; CGG is rarely used in the class of coronaviruses that can recombine with CoV-2. In fact, in the entire class of coronaviruses that includes CoV-2, the CGG-CGG combination has never been found naturally. Now the damning fact. It was this exact sequence that appears in CoV-2. Proponents of zoonotic origin must explain why the novel coronavirus, when it mutated or recombined, happened to pick its least favorite combination, the double CGG. Why did it replicate the choice the lab's gain-of-function researchers would have made? Yes, it could have happened randomly, through mutations. But do you believe that? At the minimum, this fact—that the coronavirus, with all its random possibilities, took the rare and unnatural combination used by human researchers—implies that the leading theory for the origin of the coronavirus must be laboratory escape. Best, Andrew Kerr, Investigative Reporter, Daily Caller News Foundation
